name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,348

entries.clue: Fair, as all exams should be presumably (8)

annotation.definition2: as all exams should be presumably

blocks.note: a fair effort is good enough and no better — the shrug in a school report

blocks.clueFragment: as all exams should be presumably
blocks.note: every candidate ought to be able to get through the paper set, which is the second sense of the word

annotation.surface: A remark that exams ought to be even-handed towards everybody sitting them.
annotation.walkthrough: One word twice: 'fair' judges quality, and the exam half splits into pass and -able. PASSABLE is rarely used of exams in real speech, which is why 'presumably' is there to excuse it.
annotation.definitionFit: Fair work is adequate and no more; and a paper a candidate can get through is one that can be passed — the two senses the one word carries.

entries.clue: Plant to begin with some lilac or nothing? (5)

indicatorNotes.some: 'some' asks for a part and not the whole, so only a stretch of the words beside it is wanted.

blocks.note: five letters running on from the middle of the first word, through the second and into the third

annotation.surface: A gardener given the choice between some lilac and nothing at all.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole opening phrase, not the single word 'Plant' — an oak at its very start is what is wanted. The hidden run begins inside 'lilac', which is the hardest place to see a seam.
annotation.definitionFit: The seed an oak grows from is that tree at its very beginning, so the phrase names a plant caught at the start of its life.

entries.clue: Broadcaster extremely slick? Yes, primarily (3)

indicatorNotes.extremely: 'extremely' points at the extremes of the word beside it, its first and last letters with nothing in between.
indicatorNotes.primarily: What comes primarily comes first, so only the opening letter of the word before it is taken.

blocks.note: the first and last letters of the word
the word's opening letter

annotation.surface: Someone agreeing that a thing is extremely smooth.
annotation.walkthrough: Two extraction instructions sit back to back, each aimed at the word in front of it. Sky is the British satellite company, and the answer wants a capital letter the grid will never show you.
annotation.definitionFit: The British satellite television company of that name runs channels of its own, which makes 'broadcaster' the flat trade description.

entries.clue: Club together with church collection (5)

indicatorNotes.together with: 'together with' sets one thing alongside another, so the two pieces are written out side by side.

blocks.note: a bat is a club for hitting with, in cricket or in anger
ch = church, the abbreviation used on maps and signs

annotation.surface: Clubbing together with the church over its collection.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Club together' looks like one phrase about pooling money, and the setter wants only the first word of it, meaning a stick. The collection at the end is a baker's lot, not the plate going round.
annotation.definitionFit: Loaves baked or letters handled in one go make a collection of exactly that sort — things gathered and dealt with as one lot.

entries.clue: English, strange, welcoming turncoat — mistake (7)

indicatorNotes.welcoming: To welcome somebody is to take them in, so what follows goes inside what came before it.

blocks.note: e = English, the language label a dictionary uses
rum means odd or strange — 'a rum do'
a rat is somebody who deserts his own side

annotation.surface: An eccentric Englishman making a traitor welcome.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Strange' is the standard anagram signal and here is only a synonym for odd; nothing in this clue gets shuffled. The dash is all that marks off the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A printer's mistake is exactly what the Latin word means — the thing that went wrong, owned up to on a slip pasted into the front of the book.

entries.clue: Notes place to sit (4)

blocks.note: so is the fifth note of the sol-fa scale
fa is the fourth, and the plural asks for both of them

annotation.surface: A note left for somebody telling them where to sit.
annotation.walkthrough: Sol-fa hands the crossword a set of ready-made notes — do, re, mi, fa, so — and two of them run together here. Four words of plain English, with no instruction word anywhere in them.
annotation.definitionFit: The long padded seat in a sitting room, wide enough for two or three, is the place to sit that a living room is built around.

entries.clue: Stalwart excited about eastern ocean feature (4,5)

indicatorNotes.excited: Something excited will not keep still, and letters that will not keep still do not stay in the order handed over.
indicatorNotes.about: 'about' takes the letter beside it in among the others being stirred, instead of leaving it outside them.

blocks.note: eight letters, wanted for their spelling and not their sense
e = eastern, the compass point's initial, joining the letters to be rearranged

annotation.surface: A loyal supporter worked up about something happening out east.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stalwart' sits where a solver expects a person and is eight letters of raw material, with the eastern E making a ninth. The definition is the two words at the end, which read as the last of the news.
annotation.definitionFit: What fills an ocean is brine and what fills a lake is not, so the sea is picked out here by the taste of the stuff in it.

entries.clue: Kind doctor has info (7)

indicatorNotes.doctor: To doctor a document is to tamper with it, and letters tampered with come out in an order of somebody else's choosing.

blocks.note: seven letters, taken for their spelling and not their sense

annotation.surface: A kindly doctor who has heard the news.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Kind doctor' reads as one phrase and splits between the halves of the clue: the first word defines, the second instructs. 'Kind' is the noun here — a manner or way — not the adjective the surface hands you.
annotation.definitionFit: A kind is a manner or way of doing a thing, and the answer's older sense is exactly that: the way in which something is done.

entries.clue: Thin scientific study of plants — no cheers at centre (4)

indicatorNotes.no: 'no' says the thing named next is not there, so those letters never reach the answer.
indicatorNotes.at centre: 'at centre' says where the missing pair were sitting — in the middle of the longer word, not at either end.

blocks.note: botany is the science of plants
ta is British for thanks, and 'cheers' is said in the same breath and means the same thing

annotation.surface: A slight study of plant science that gets no applause.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cheers' is the British way of saying thank you as well as a toast, which is what puts TA in the middle of the longer word. 'Thin' leads the clue, where it reads as a verdict on the study.
annotation.definitionFit: Somebody thin has little flesh on them and the skeleton shows through, which is what the word describes.

entries.clue: Indefatigable, lively sister captivating the French (8)

indicatorNotes.lively: Something lively will not keep still, and letters that will not keep still do not stay in the order given.
indicatorNotes.captivating: To captivate somebody is to take them prisoner, so what follows is held inside the letters before it.

blocks.note: the six letters of sister in another order
le is the French word for 'the', masculine singular

annotation.surface: A high-spirited nun who has the French entranced.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sister' is a nun on the surface and six letters to be shuffled in the wordplay, with the French 'le' dropped into the middle of them. 'Captivating' means charm on the surface and imprisonment in the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: Somebody indefatigable never flags, and the word says it from the other end — by the weariness that never arrives.

entries.clue: Speaks sharply, furious — quick assessment (8)

blocks.note: to snap at somebody is to speak sharply to them
hot under the collar is furious — hot tempers, hot words

annotation.surface: Somebody barking at people in a rage.
annotation.walkthrough: Both wordplay words are ordinary anger words, so the sentence never breaks step. The definition borrows the photographer's sense: a snapshot of opinion is a reading taken on the spot and not touched up.
annotation.definitionFit: A quick assessment is a picture caught in one instant and left as it came out, which is what a pollster means by the word.

entries.clue: Example from past — physical training going around playground garden (9)

indicatorNotes.going around: Something going around another thing is wrapped about it, so the two letters before must split and enclose what follows.

blocks.note: PT is the school timetable's name for physical training
in Britain a rec is the local recreation ground, the field and swings where children play
Eden is the garden of Genesis

annotation.surface: A gym class jogging round the park and the flower beds.
annotation.walkthrough: The wrapper splits, one letter going in front and one behind, which is the step that hides the short PT. A rec is a British recreation ground, so 'playground' asks for the field rather than the swings on it.
annotation.definitionFit: An earlier case a court can point to decides what happens now, so an example from the past is exactly what the word names in law.

entries.clue: With that fellow? Fancy! (4)

blocks.note: w = with, the shorthand of recipes and scribbled notes
'that fellow' is the man already mentioned

annotation.surface: Surprise at finding somebody in that man's company.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fancy!' is an exclamation of surprise on the surface and a noun in the answer, as in a passing fancy. Both question mark and exclamation mark are punctuation the solver can ignore.
annotation.definitionFit: A fancy is a notion that takes hold for no reason and passes just as quickly, which is the impulse the answer names.

entries.clue: Notice odd one out, the fanatic, strangest ultimately (6)

indicatorNotes.ultimately: 'ultimately' points at the end of things, so only the closing letter of each word before it is taken.

blocks.clueFragment: odd one out, the fanatic, strangest
blocks.note: the last letter of each of those six words, read in the order they come

annotation.surface: Spotting the strangest of the zealots, the one who does not belong.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Odd one out' is a phrase here and not an instruction to drop anything, which is the false trail. Six words each give up a last letter, and the commas make the list look like a description rather than a queue of letters.
annotation.definitionFit: To notice a fault, a smell or a movement is to pick it out from everything around it, and the verb carries that plain sense as well as the detective's.

entries.clue: Zoom in general needs updating (7)

indicatorNotes.needs updating: What needs updating is not right as it stands and has to be rebuilt, so the word beside it is put together again another way.

blocks.note: seven letters, wanted for their spelling and not their rank

annotation.surface: A general who has fallen behind the times and needs bringing up to date.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In' belongs to the definition rather than joining the two halves, so 'Zoom in' has to be read as one verb from a camera. Nothing of the army survives the shuffle.
annotation.definitionFit: Zooming in on a picture makes what you are looking at bigger, which is the plain job of the verb.

entries.clue: One making effort to accommodate former Queen’s dog (7)

indicatorNotes.to accommodate: To accommodate somebody is to find room for them indoors, so the letters named are taken inside the word before.

blocks.note: somebody who has a go at things is a trier
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the late Queen's signature, and 'former' marks the reign as ended

annotation.surface: A hard worker finding room for the late Queen's pet.
annotation.walkthrough: Elizabeth II kept corgis, so the surface points at the wrong small breed while you count letters. ER is the regnal signature, the monarch's initial with Regina or Rex behind it.
annotation.definitionFit: The breed was made small to go down holes after foxes and badgers, so 'dog' names it by the wider class it belongs to.

entries.clue: Greek character, diminutive, in act of defiance (6)

blocks.note: mu is the twelfth letter of the Greek alphabet
diminutive means tiny

annotation.surface: A very small Greek caught up in a rebellion.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Greek character' is the alphabet and not a man from Athens, and mu is the letter wanted. The commas do all the joining, so 'in' is the one link and hands over nothing.
annotation.definitionFit: Sailors who refuse the captain's orders and seize the ship commit precisely that act of defiance against lawful authority.

entries.clue: University rower, maybe, not happy (4)

blocks.note: at Oxford and Cambridge the award for representing the university against the other is named after a colour, and whoever holds it takes the name too
the colour English has used for low spirits for centuries

annotation.surface: An Oxbridge oarsman in low spirits.
annotation.walkthrough: A Blue is the award Oxford and Cambridge give for representing the university, and the Boat Race is where the country sees them. 'Maybe' flags the rower as one instance of a Blue rather than the whole of it.
annotation.definitionFit: Somebody who rows for Oxford or Cambridge earns the award named for the university colours; and the same word has meant downcast in English for centuries.

entries.clue: Retiring soldiers were in the army? (8)

blocks.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, the army's sappers and the crossword's usual soldiers
to serve is to be in the forces, and this is the past tense of it

annotation.surface: Old soldiers stepping down after a career in uniform.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Retiring' means shy here, though the surface makes it the end of a career. The question mark nods at the Army Reserve, whose soldiers are indeed in the army.
annotation.definitionFit: Somebody retiring keeps to themselves and holds back in company, which is the quiet manner the word describes.

entries.clue: Relative introducing a learner where hair’s done (5)

indicatorNotes.introducing: To introduce somebody is to bring them in, so what follows goes inside the word before it.

blocks.note: a son is a relative
the word itself, taken as it stands
L is the plate a learner driver has to display in Britain

annotation.surface: A family member taking a beginner along to the hairdresser's.
annotation.walkthrough: The insertion lands after the first letter, so the relative is split almost as soon as it starts. Two pieces go in together, which is unusual enough to be worth watching for.
annotation.definitionFit: The room a hairdresser works in borrows the French word for a drawing room, and it is where hair gets cut, coloured and set.

entries.clue: Dodge first lady to bring commercial material in? (5)

indicatorNotes.to bring: To bring something is to carry it along with you, and here it carries the letters named over to the word already in place.
indicatorNotes.in: 'in' says the carried letters finish up inside that word rather than beside it.

blocks.note: Eve is the first woman of Genesis
ad = an advertisement, the commercial matter a page or a broadcast carries

annotation.surface: Sidestepping a first lady who turns up carrying advertising copy.
annotation.walkthrough: 'First lady' points at the White House and means Genesis, where Eve is the crossword's first woman. The question mark covers 'commercial material', which is a roundabout way of asking for two letters.
annotation.definitionFit: To dodge a question or a tax is to get out of its way by ducking and weaving, which is what the verb means.

entries.clue: What provides choice of fewer suffering and ailing? (4,4)

indicatorNotes.suffering: Something suffering is in a bad way and no longer as it was, so the letters beside it come out in another order.

blocks.note: the five letters of fewer in another order
somebody ailing is ill

annotation.surface: Something that lets you choose how many people suffer and sicken.
annotation.walkthrough: The chunks straddle the gap between the answer's two words, so the split the enumeration promises never lines up with the wordplay. 'Suffering' and 'ailing' look like a matched pair and only one of them is an instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: The doctrine that a person's choices are their own and not settled in advance is the philosophers' name for what provides choice.

entries.clue: Signify penny-pinching (4)

blocks.note: what a word does when it stands for something — 'and what does that signify?'
counting every penny out of tightness, which is the British charge rather than the American one of nastiness

annotation.surface: A sign that somebody is being tight with money.
annotation.walkthrough: Two words, two definitions, and no join at all between them — one a verb, the other an adjective, which is why they refuse to settle into a sentence. The stingy sense is the British one.
annotation.definitionFit: To signify is what a word or a sign does when it stands for something; and somebody penny-pinching is tight-fisted, the everyday British charge of stinginess.

entries.clue: By sound of it, short time cut (3)

indicatorNotes.By sound of it: 'By sound of it' asks for what the ear hears and not what the page shows, so the answer is spelt differently from the word named.

blocks.note: a mo is a moment, British for the shortest stretch of time there is — 'hang on a mo'

annotation.surface: A brief moment being cut short.
annotation.walkthrough: Three letters, and only one of them changes between what is said and what is written, which is exactly why the sound has to be pointed out. The definition is the last word on its own.
annotation.definitionFit: Cutting grass down to an even height is the whole job of the verb, which is why a lawn gets one every week in summer.

entries.clue: Broken step — nuisance (4)

indicatorNotes.Broken: Something broken has come apart, and the letters beside it get put back together in a new order.

blocks.note: four letters, wanted for their spelling and not their sense

annotation.surface: A cracked step on the stairs, and what a bother it is.
annotation.walkthrough: Four-letter anagrams hide best because there is so little to rearrange, and 'Broken step' reads as one ordinary household complaint. The dash does the work of an equals sign.
annotation.definitionFit: A nuisance is whatever keeps bothering you, and the word covers the wasp at the picnic as readily as the child who will not stop asking.

entries.clue: Wonder about including European name, famous (8)

indicatorNotes.about: Letters sent about are sent every which way, so the word beside it does not keep the order it came in.
indicatorNotes.including: 'including' takes the two letters named into the same handful being rearranged instead of leaving them outside it.

blocks.note: six letters, taken for their spelling and not their sense
e = European, as on an EU label
n = name, the abbreviation on a form

annotation.surface: Wondering about the name of a well-known European.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Wonder about' reads as idle pondering and is the instruction; the two single letters joining in are what stretch six letters to eight. The comma before the last word is the only sign the definition has begun.
annotation.definitionFit: Somebody famous is spoken of again and again by people who never met them, which is what the word says in its own roots.
